Abstract: Due to the ever-increasing consumption of resources, various materials and raw materials have become increasingly scarce and consequently expensive. At the same time, energy demand has dramatically increased in global mining operations also intensifying economic pressure. Surprisingly, the recapturing of important raw materials at the end of the product life cycle through recycling is still insufficiently implemented in the supply chain. Recycling is not only a sink for unwanted materials it can become an urban mine. This is especially relevant in Europe, where in comparison to other continents primary raw material mining of bulk materials is rather low. In a situation of scarcity, the exact planning of raw material and material flows for the following months (and sometimes years) has become ever more vital to ensure their timely and sufficient availability for production. A missing piece is the necessary transfer of production information (like bill of materials, BOM) to the recycler because information is typically kept inside the production supply chain. Digital technologies such as Digital Twins can help provide this information to the End-of-Life (EoL) stakeholders (recycling industry) as a means to increase the potential of circular economy. This paper establishes urban mining as an important concept of life cycle management in the circular economy. It uses a case study approach to explore the potential of urban mining for resource savings. The authors demonstrate that urban mining represents a high-impact application of sustainable engineering within life cycle management where Digital Twins help increase impact on sustainability.

Abstract: The rapid diffusion of cyber-physical systems (CPS), digital twins, and data-driven architectures has reconfigured manufacturing systems under the Industry 4.0 paradigm, while the emerging Industry 5.0 perspective emphasizes human-centricity, sustainability, and resilience. This paper presents a PRISMA-guided systematic survey combined with taxonomy-building and conceptual synthesis of CPS-enabled and digital twin-supported human-centric manufacturing systems. The paper also positions the proposed taxonomy against prior reviews, classifies digital twin implementations according to maturity level, functionality, and lifecycle integration, and distinguishes empirically supported outcomes from conceptual or expected benefits. Abstract: Agentic AI systems — where large language models (LLMs) autonomously plan, reason, and act — are emerging as a compelling paradigm for managing the complexity of optical networks [1, 2]. Two independent design axes shape any such system. The first is autonomy: whether the LLM freely sequences tool calls and decides when to stop (ReAct-style open loop [3]), or whether control flow is pre-encoded as a deterministic graph, with the LLM invoked only at fixed decision points. The second is application programming interface (API) abstraction: whether the agent interacts with the network through semantic, domain-specific tools that encapsulate protocol details (high abstraction) or through raw protocol primitives that require the LLM to construct RESTCONF paths, resolve UUIDs, and parse nested YANG-model JSON directly (low abstraction). Note that high API abstraction reduces the LLM’s reasoning burden at the tool-call level, whereas low API abstraction demands greater in-context synthesis from the LLM — a distinction that is important when interpreting accuracy differences across LLM variants. Prior demonstrations over NETCONF/YANG [4] and OpenConfig [5] have shown the feasibility of LLM agents in optical network management, but none have characterized the architectural trade-offs that follow from these two choices. The gap matters: operators deploying agents on live infrastructure need to know which position in this design space best fits their requirements for generality, predictability, and trustworthiness. This paper makes two contributions. First, it establishes the autonomy × abstraction framework as basis for reasoning about agentic AI design choices in optical networking, covering all four quadrants of the design space. Second, it grounds the framework in three concrete implementations over the same T-API [6] digital twin: (i) a high-autonomy, high-abstraction ReAct agent with 18 domain-specific tools covering topology queries, optical performance monitoring (OPM), quality of transmission (QoT) analysis, and network (re)configuration across 12 scenarios; (ii) a low-autonomy, high-abstraction directed graph workflow that constrains the LLM to fixed invocations within a compiled agent graph with fully deterministic branching, including a modulation format cascade (DP-64QAM → DP-16QAM → DP-QPSK) executed without any LLM involvement; and (iii) a highautonomy, low-abstraction variant that replaces the 18 domain tools with 2 generic HTTP primitives, requiring the LLM to construct raw T-API RESTCONF paths, resolve UUID references, and navigate nested YANG-model JSON directly. The low-autonomy, low-abstraction quadrant — a directed graph calling raw protocol endpoints — exists conceptually but offers no practical advantage over the other three concrete implementations and is left as a boundary case. The three implementations are compared across five dimensions, three structural and two empirical. Generality: the high-autonomy ReAct agent handles all 12 scenario types covering topology queries, OPM, path analysis, lightpath provisioning, and multi-turn management; the directed graph handles lightpath provisioning only, evaluated across 100 randomly sampled node pairs from the CORONET CONUS topology. Predictability: every execution path of the directed graph is a deterministic function of typed state and fully enumerable at design time; the ReAct agents produce traces determined at inference time with unbounded tool-call sequences. Constraint enforcement: the directed graph embeds domain rules in branching logic the LLM never sees, enforced independently of model quality; both ReAct variants rely on the system prompt, making enforcement contingent on model compliance. Human oversight: the low-abstraction tools require the user to interpret low-level messages exchanged between the agent and the network controller, while the high-abstraction set of tools allow more precise human oversight due to each tool being linked to a specific functionality. Token cost: we measure how many tokens are necessary for each system realization to achieve a pre-defined set of goals as a representation of the cost to accomplish the tasks. Three key outcomes can be mentioned. High autonomy should be preferred when task diversity is high, and the full set of management scenarios cannot be anticipated at design time. Low autonomy should be preferred when predictability and auditability are safety requirements, or when domain constraints must be enforced independently of model behavior. On the abstraction axis, high API abstraction consistently reduces LLM error surface, prompt complexity, and operator evaluation burden; the engineering cost of building domain-specific tools is recovered in reliability and is progressively offset as interfaces such as T-API and model context protocol (MCP) standardize semantic operations at the protocol level.

Abstract: The emergence of the Metaverse as a persistent, immersive, and interoperable digital ecosystem introduces system-level challenges in identity management, security, and privacy protection across networked extended reality environments.
